note: Hand-picked, not derived. The rule: a term earns a place only if knowing it changes how you can describe something in ordinary English. Excluded on purpose - taxonomic Latin, unit names, anything whose technical sense contradicts its everyday one, and jargon that cannot travel outside its field. 'pknown'/'zipf' are only used for words absent from the prevalence norms; where the norms have the word, the measured values win.

words.note: The whole horizontal band a classical colonnade carries - architrave, frieze and cornice together.
The lowest band of the entablature; also the moulded frame around a door or window.
The projecting crown at the top of a wall. The word survives in ordinary speech for the moulding at a ceiling.
The triangular gable over a portico. A broken pediment is one interrupted at the apex.
A flattened column engaged in a wall - structure implied rather than performed.
A bracket of stone or brick stepped out from a wall to carry a load.
The near-triangular surface between an arch and its frame; in a curtain wall, the opaque panel between floors.

words.def: The underside of an architectural element such as an eave, arch or balcony
words.note: The word planners reach for when they mean 'the bit you see looking up'.

words.def: The arrangement of windows and openings in a facade
words.note: Not just 'windows' - the pattern of them, which is what makes a facade read as ordered or restless.
A run of high windows above roof level, bringing light deep into a room without giving a view in.

words.def: A vertical bar dividing the lights of a window
words.note: The vertical one. Horizontal is a transom - a distinction people mix up constantly.
The horizontal bar across a window or above a door; also the small window it frames.
The beam over an opening. The oldest structural idea there is, and still the commonest.
The vertical side of a door or window opening.
The depth of wall between the face and the window in it. A deep reveal reads as mass; a flush one as skin.

words.def: One of the wedge-shaped stones forming an arch
words.note: The keystone is only the most famous voussoir.
The wedge at the crown of an arch that locks the rest in place - hence the metaphor.
The recessed face within a pediment or over a door, usually where the carving goes.
The middle band of an entablature; more loosely, any decorated horizontal strip.
The base a column, statue or building sits on. Useful for buildings: a plinth is how a tower meets the street.
A railing carried on short posts - balusters. A parapet is solid; a balustrade is open.
The low wall carried up past the roof. It hides the roof and fixes the building's silhouette.
A small dome crowning a roof, usually more about the skyline than the room below.
A row of columns carrying an entablature. An arcade does the same job with arches.
A run of arches on piers or columns; by extension, the covered walk it forms.
A room open along one side to the air - a gallery that is neither inside nor out.
A roofed entrance porch carried on columns.
The entrance vestibule across the front of a church - the compression before the nave opens up.
The central body of a church, between the aisles.
A semicircular recess, usually vaulted, closing the end of a nave.
A mass built against a wall to take the outward thrust. Flying when it does so across a gap.
A round opening, especially at the crown of a dome. The Pantheon's is the definitive one.
A sunken panel in a ceiling or vault - lighter structure and better acoustics, incidentally beautiful.

words.def: A dressed stone at the external corner of a building
words.note: Quoins announce a corner. Their absence is what makes a modern box read as taut.

words.def: Squared, finely dressed stone laid in regular courses
words.note: The opposite of rubble. Ashlar is the expensive way to say a wall is deliberate.

words.def: Masonry cut with deep joints and a rough face, usually at the base of a building
words.note: Weight at the bottom, refinement above - a rhetorical device, not a structural one.
A roof with two pitches on each side, the lower one steep - a way of getting a storey past a height limit.
The barn version of a mansard, with the double pitch on two sides only.
A window standing up out of a sloping roof, with its own small roof.
The overhanging edge of a roof. The eaves line, more than the peak, is what sets a street's scale.

words.def: The triangular upper part of a wall closing the end of a pitched roof
words.note: The triangle of wall closing the end of a pitched roof.

words.def: A bay window projecting from an upper storey and carried on brackets
words.note: A bay window that never reaches the ground.
A beam fixed at one end only. Structurally demanding, rhetorically irresistible.
A framework of triangles spanning further than a beam of the same weight could.
One of the parallel beams carrying a floor or ceiling.

words.def: A horizontal beam running along the length of a roof, supporting the rafters
A bevelled edge, made by cutting away a square corner at 45 degrees
words.note: A chamfered corner at a street intersection is a planning instrument, not just a detail.
The plate around a keyhole or handle; in heraldry, the shield itself.

words.def: A floor finish of stone chips set in cement and ground smooth
words.note: Chips of stone set in cement and ground smooth - the floor of every mid-century civic building.
Render used as a finish, often modelled. It lets a cheap wall imitate an expensive one.

words.def: To break away in flakes or chips, as concrete or stone does when it weathers or corrodes
words.note: Spalling concrete is the visible half of a reinforcement problem.
The white salt bloom on masonry left as water moves through and evaporates. Also the general sense: a flowering.
The surface a material earns through age. Distinguishable from dirt mainly by intention.

words.def: The overall three-dimensional bulk and shape of a building, before any detail
words.note: The single most useful word in a design review: it separates form from finish.
The way a large surface is broken into readable parts. Unarticulated mass is the usual complaint.
The distance a building is held back from a lot line, or the step in a facade as it rises.

words.def: A suite of rooms aligned so their doorways form a single vista
words.note: A device for making a house feel like a procession.
An intermediate floor, partial by definition - it overlooks rather than encloses.
A top-lit space rising through several storeys. Roman houses had one open to the sky.
Building in the local idiom, by custom rather than by design. The word carries no condescension unless you add it.
A surface reused so that earlier marks still show through. The standard metaphor for a city that has been rebuilt on itself.

words.def: The route people actually take, worn into the ground regardless of the path provided
words.note: The most honest post-occupancy evaluation there is.
How easily people can move through a block or area. Long blocks are impermeable however wide the pavements.
How readily a place can be read and navigated. Lynch's term, and still the right one.
The texture of a built area - fine grain means many small parcels and frequent doors.
A reference line a composition is measured against; in survey, the level everything else is relative to.

words.def: The solid, inhabited thickness of a wall as shown blacked in on a plan
words.note: The Beaux-Arts insight: walls are not lines, they are places.

words.def: A fixed screen of fins or louvres shading a facade from the sun
A non-structural outer skin hung from the building's frame
words.note: It carries nothing but itself - which is why it can be all glass.
An arched ceiling. Barrel, groin and fan describe how the arches meet.
The outer layer applied to a structure. After Grenfell the word does a great deal of work it did not used to.
Which way a room or dwelling faces. Dual aspect means light and air from two sides, and it is the difference between a good flat and a bad one.
The measure of disorder, and of energy unavailable to do work. Used loosely for decay, which is close enough to be forgivable.
Something that speeds a reaction without being consumed. The metaphor holds precisely: a catalyst is unchanged by what it causes.
Same element, different neutron count. What makes carbon dating possible.
The rate at which a quantity changes across space. Temperature, pressure, rent - all have gradients.
The level at which something begins to happen. Below it, nothing; above it, everything.
Output looping back to become input. Negative feedback stabilises; positive feedback runs away.
A property the whole has that no part has. Traffic jams are emergent; so are cities.

words.def: Governed by chance; describable only in terms of probabilities
words.note: Not the same as random: a stochastic process has structure, just not determinacy.
The maintenance of a stable internal state against a changing outside.
The delay between cause and observable effect.

words.def: The lag in a system's response, so that its state depends on its history as well as its inputs
words.note: Why a market that fell does not simply reverse when conditions return.
To reduce in force or intensity. Signals, sound and stormwater flows are all attenuated.
Spreading from high concentration to low, without anything pushing.
Allowing passage through. In surfaces, the property that decides whether rain soaks in or runs off.

words.def: The fraction of sunlight a surface reflects rather than absorbs
words.note: The whole urban heat island argument in one measurement.
The total mass of living material in a given area.
To set apart and hold. Carbon is sequestered; so, differently, is a jury.

words.def: Caused by human activity
words.note: The word that does the arguing in most climate sentences.

words.def: Of or on the bank of a river or watercourse
words.note: Riparian rights and riparian habitat are two different bodies of thought sharing an adjective.

words.def: Deposited by flowing water, as on a floodplain or delta
words.note: Deposited by running water. Alluvial soil is why floodplains are farmed and then built on.
A body of rock or sediment holding groundwater that can be drawn from.
The area draining to a single point. The metaphorical sense - a turning point - comes from the ridge, not the basin.
The sinking of ground, whether from extraction below or consolidation of soft ground.
Material carried by water and set down when it slows.

words.def: The climate of a very small area where it differs from the region around it
words.note: Local conditions that depart from the regional pattern - the reason one plaza is unusable in March.

words.def: The amount of solar radiation reaching a surface
words.note: One letter from insulation and nearly its opposite concern.
Existing as tiny separate particles. PM2.5 is a particulate measure and a public health one.
A quantity with both size and direction; separately, the organism that carries a disease.

words.def: Growing by a constant proportion each period, and so ever faster in absolute terms
words.note: Growing by a constant proportion, not a constant amount. Almost always used loosely to mean 'fast'.

words.def: Approaching a value ever more closely without ever reaching it

words.note: To vary together. Carries no claim about cause, which is the whole difficulty.

words.def: Of a third variable that distorts an apparent relationship between two others
words.note: The reason most observed relationships are not what they look like.

words.def: The effect where a small amount of noise makes a weak signal easier to detect

words.note: The capacity to absorb disturbance and keep functioning. Not the same as resistance, which refuses the disturbance instead.
Spare capacity that does nothing until something fails. The most undervalued property of any system.
A state in which opposing influences balance. Nothing about it implies stability or desirability.
Of the chemical processes sustaining life. 'Urban metabolism' borrows the term to track a city's flows of energy and matter.
Two organisms living together to mutual benefit. Often used where 'coexistence' is meant.

words.def: The transition zone between two ecological communities
words.note: Edges are where the diversity is - true of habitats and, arguably, neighbourhoods.
Native to and confined to a place. In disease, constantly present - which is not the same as an epidemic.
A remnant of something that once had a function.

words.def: Relating to the balance of the earth's crust floating on the mantle
words.note: Isostatic rebound is why parts of Canada are still rising after the ice left.
A fluid's resistance to flow.
Of or relating to being pulled. Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension, which is why it is reinforced.
Force acting to slide one layer past another. Shear walls exist to resist it.
Twisting under load.
The turning effect of a force about a point - force times distance. Nothing to do with time.
The rate of flow through a surface; also, more loosely, continuous change.

words.def: To add a measured reagent little by little until a reaction is complete
words.note: To add a reagent by small measured amounts until a reaction completes - hence, to adjust a dose carefully.
To pass from solid straight to vapour; in psychology, to redirect an impulse into acceptable work.
To bring on suddenly; in chemistry, to come out of solution as a solid. Both senses share the sense of falling out.
